texts: good. the tide, the rising and the twice-a-day rate are all carried, with no tense invented on a habit.

bad: 'of the lunar cycle' forces a part-of link from the kind 'spring tides' to one particular cycle, which mixes kinds and individuals, so the compliant reading has to drop it; and the definite 'the large tides' — that they are exactly the large ones — has no carrier either way. Make the cycle a condition on the property instead: 'Spring tides are large in the lunar cycle.' That shape is recorded (the property holds within that cycle), so only the exhaustiveness is lost rather than the cycle as well.
good. 'occur' correctly puts the times straight on the tide rather than inventing a separate happening, and the either/or is kept narrow and inclusive as the sentence states it.

mixed: the whenever-rule itself is exactly right — the filling is the trigger, the blooming is a fresh event tied to it, and it can fire. But 'salt-bloom' and the verb 'blooms' reduce to the same word, so the record ends up saying the substance salt-bloom is a kind of blooming. Use a different verb for the event: 'Whenever a spring tide fills the Salt-bloom Tide-pools, salt-bloom flowers in the pools.'

mixed: only 'neap tides are small' is recorded — the definite 'the small tides', i.e. that the small ones are exactly the neap ones, has no carrier and is lost. Nothing currently recovers that identity claim, so if the property is all you need write 'Neap tides are small.', which promises exactly what is kept.

good. 'occur' puts the time straight on the tide and the claim reads as a general rule about neap tides; the quarter-moon time slot is improvised territory in the instruction set, but nothing false is recorded.
good. the neap tide, the tide-pools, the leaving and the resulting dryness are all carried, with the dryness handed to each pool rather than to the set as a whole.

mixed: 'a spring-tide fill' mints one particular fill and so records that such a fill exists, which 'needs' does not claim; and a bare mass subject with a singular object leaves the general-claim route undecided. Make the object a bare plural so both sides are kinds: 'Salt-bloom needs spring-tide fills.' That records the requirement between the two kinds without claiming any particular filling happened.
